query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature tribocorrosion conditions, differential oxidation/galling at phase boundaries in the multi-phase eutectic HEA produces mechanically unstable oxide films that, when ruptured by wear, expose fresh material and create localized galvanic cells. This synergy accelerates the overall degradation compared to isolated wear or corrosion mechanisms.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a refined microstructure comprising distinct phases (e.g., an FCC matrix and a σ phase) that exhibit different oxidation behaviors.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA to simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive attack in an aggressive environment (such as a 3.5 wt.% NaCl electrolyte) at an elevated temperature (~300°C), while controlling oxygen partial pressure and chloride content.
generation.conditions: The tests are performed under a continuous mechanical load (to induce wear) and in a corrosive electrolyte at high temperature. A controlled comparison is set up where the alloy is subjected separately to wear-only and corrosion-only conditions under otherwise identical environmental conditions, to serve as a matched baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfacial phase chemistry—specifically, the differential oxidation behavior at the boundaries between the distinct phases (e.g., between FCC and σ phases) leading to non-uniform, weak oxide films and subsequent localized galvanic effects.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the distinct phases oxidize at different rates. This results in the formation of an unstable oxide film at the phase boundaries. Under mechanical loading, the mechanically compromised oxide film ruptures, exposing fresh metal and promoting localized galvanic corrosion between the oxidized and less oxidized regions. This feedback loop of film rupture and localized corrosion accelerates degradation beyond the sum of the individual wear and corrosion contributions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the matched baseline (with only wear or corrosion active), the total degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion is predicted to be significantly higher. Specifically, there will be an increase in abrasive wear due to intermittent oxide film rupture and an enhanced corrosion rate at the phase boundaries due to localized galvanic cells, resulting in more severe wear tracks and higher pit densities.
generation.baseline: A matched alloy sample exposed separately to wear-only conditions (mechanical stress without electrolyte) and corrosion-only conditions (electrochemical attack without mechanical loading) under identical high-temperature settings.
generation.boundary: Elevated temperature (around 300°C) in a chloride-rich corrosive environment under continuous mechanical loading; the microstructure should remain stable (i.e., without phase transformations) during the duration of the experiment.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative enhancement of degradation (both wear and corrosion rates) due to the coupled effect is uncertain and likely sensitive to specific environmental parameters (e.g., oxygen partial pressure, chloride ion concentration) and exact phase compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ tribocorrosion experiments on the HEA at ~300°C under controlled chloride and oxygen environments. Prepare two sets of samples: one with the native heterogeneous phase boundaries and a second with modified interfacial chemistry (e.g., via micro-alloying or heat treatment) aimed at homogenizing the oxidation response. Compare the total mass loss, wear track morphology, and corrosion rates between the two groups and with isolated wear-only and corrosion-only tests.
measurements: Total mass loss over time under simultaneous wear-corrosion conditions
Wear track depth and morphology using scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Electrochemical measurements of corrosion current density and pit density
High-speed imaging or in situ monitoring of oxide film formation/rupture events
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If altering the interfacial phase chemistry to homogenize oxidation behavior does not lead to a significant reduction in the synergistic acceleration of degradation (i.e., if combined wear-corrosion degradation remains comparable to the sum of isolated wear and corrosion effects), or if degradation under simultaneous exposure is not significantly higher than under isolated conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Boron incorporation improves the coating’s microhardness and wear resistance, with the highest wear resistance achieved at x = 1, where abrasive and oxidative wear predominate. chosen.technique: in situ tribocorrosion testing combined with electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and complementary microscopic analysis
chosen.conditions: exposing multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloys to simultaneous wear and corrosion at ~300°C in a chloride-rich electrolyte while systematically varying mechanical load to isolate the effect of local galvanic interactions
chosen.why: This move directly targets the open question by testing the hypothesis that accelerated degradation arises from thermally activated differential oxidation at phase boundaries, leading to localized galvanic effects that synergistically amplify wear and corrosion. By controlling the interfacial chemistry through a variable mechanical load and thermal conditions, the experiment distinguishes this mechanism from separate degradation modes. The design predicts that compared to a baseline alloy with minimized interfacial galvanic activity, total degradation will increase with pronounced wear and corrosion responses, and a clear falsification criterion is provided if decoupling of wear from corrosion is observed.

frame.system: The material system is a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy that begins as a complex microstructure (with distinct, coexisting phases typical of eutectic systems) and is exposed to simultaneous mechanical wear and electrochemical corrosion at elevated temperatures.
frame.goal: To develop a single mechanistic hypothesis that explains why the simultaneous action of wear and corrosion at high temperature accelerates degradation, detailing the interplay between mechanical and chemical processes compared to a baseline condition.
frame.limitation: There is an incomplete understanding of the synergistic effects between wear and corrosion in multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloys at elevated temperatures, particularly why the degradation accelerates when these mechanisms occur simultaneously, and no single hypothesis has yet unified these effects.
constraints: The hypothesis must be mechanistic and singular in nature, accounting for both wear and corrosion as interrelated processes
It requires a controlled experimental or theoretical comparison capable of distinguishing this explanation
It must predict changes in total degradation and the individual contributions from wear and corrosion relative to a matched baseline
Clear definition of relevant boundary conditions is needed
Supporting evidence must be identified and a clear falsification criterion provided
frame.regime: The alloy is subjected to high-temperature conditions where both mechanical wear (e.g., contact stresses and abrasion) and corrosive environments (e.g., aggressive electrolytes, oxidizing conditions) are simultaneously active.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have either isolated wear or corrosion, failing to capture the synergy when both are present
Baseline comparisons have been made with materials under single degradation modes, which did not reveal the coupled acceleration observed in the multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy

decision.trend: The early literature on high-entropy alloys began by optimizing eutectic microstructures for mechanical performance and high‐temperature strength (e.g., the 2014 study on eutectic HEAs and the 2017 work on high-temperature creep). Next, researchers turned to high temperature wear behavior where phenomena like the formation and catastrophic rupture of oxide films and dynamic amorphization in ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layers were identified (as seen in PMC7515071). More recent studies (e.g., PMC12156342 and PMC12565319) started to focus on coupled degradation by observing how processing methods and microalloying (such as controlled laser cladding and boron additions) affect the interfacial phase chemistry. They revealed that differences in oxidation or galling between distinct phases likely govern the transition from a relatively benign wear or corrosion response—studied separately—to an accelerated, synergistic degradation when both processes are active at elevated temperatures. However, despite these insights, precisely isolating the interfacial reactions under simultaneous wear and corrosion conditions remains unsolved.
decision.unsolved: A singular mechanistic explanation that conclusively links the differential oxidation or galling at the phase boundaries (i.e. interfacial phase chemistry) of a multi-phase eutectic HEA to the accelerated degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion at high temperatures remains as an open question. In particular, it is not yet clear how these interfacial reactions drive the marked increase in total degradation and what the individual contributions of mechanical wear versus electrochemical corrosion are when compared to a matched baseline.
decision.lever: interfacial phase chemistry (i.e. differential oxidation/galling at phase boundaries)
decision.why: Building on the trend where initial studies observed conventional wear or corrosion, and later work began to hint that phase-boundary processes (via differential oxidation) play a critical role, the most plausible next step is a controlled variable experiment. This experiment would systematically manipulate the local environment (e.g., chloride content and oxygen partial pressure) during in situ tribocorrosion tests at ~300°C under a managed mechanical load. By targeting the interfacial phase chemistry lever, the experiment aims to directly isolate and quantify the impact of differential oxidation/galling at phase boundaries, thus explaining the acceleration of coupled degradation. This approach fits the niche move in explaining why the amplified degradation occurs and provides clear predictions and falsification criteria based on changes observed in total wear, corrosion rates, and their interplay relative to a baseline condition.
